doc.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Banjo band, first gigs and first pay
summary: He started with a banjo band, got rides from older musicians, earned twenty dollars and a meal for his first gig, and laments stagnant rates.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Jeepers. So going from hearing these tunes to actually trying to play them, you have to enlist some people to play with. Do you find people who are already playing and trying to get in with them.

Yeah. Absolutely. I started out with this basically, for lack of better words, a banjo band and they used to have a lot of those banjo parlors in the world at that time, the sixties I guess, and tons of banjo players and a bass player of sort and they were so happy to see me that I was a young fellow and I would be interested in trying to learn tunes and learn chord changes. And you know, I made mistakes and there were a lot of musicians in there who weren’t that great, but you’d try to find which musician is the better one. And then eventually one fellow came to me and said, “hey you want to do a gig?” “A gig, sure.” And so my dad used to take me around, because I was too young to drive, and eventually I would meet musicians who were older, like 17 or 18, you know these were older guys. And they were able to pick me up and bring me to the gigs. And since I was this tall and a kind of heavy fellow, I was never carded or questioned. I seemed to look old enough to be part of the night life.
Do you remember what the first dollar amount that you ever made was?
As a professional musician I think it was twenty dollars for the evening, plus a meal.
It’s not too bad. It’s not too bad today.
I know, it felt pretty good at that time.
I mean I think the music business is the only business that the musicians’ rates are either the same or worse than they were thirty years ago. It’s the truth. It’s a very sad commentary. But anyway.
